introduction: “Do not worship the Lantern—worship the light.” The guide holds that sentence together with its opposite number, Shoghi Effendi’s insistence that to accept the Cause without its administration is to accept half of it. Between them lie warnings against committees, clergy, paid ministers, rule-making and “over-administration”, and arguments that a world-wide community needs elected bodies, coordinated authority and a pattern to offer a disordered age. The tension is as old as religion with a second generation. Paul tells Corinth that everyone may bring a psalm and also that all must be done decently and in order; the apostles appoint seven so as to stay free for prayer; Jethro tells Moses he will wear himself away; Jesus keeps the sabbath for man and warns against heavy burdens and tithed mint. Political thinkers supply the cautions: Acton on power, Madison on men who are not angels, Montesquieu on united powers, Mill on the state that dwarfs its men. And Blake, Dickinson, Paine and Rousseau speak for those who would do without the lantern altogether.
questions: Paul wants “every one” to contribute and “all things … decently and in order”. How do the first readings, with their formless meetings, and the later ones, with their Assemblies, divide the same ground?
The apostles appointed seven to serve tables so that they could keep to prayer and teaching. Does that episode support reading 11’s contrast between organizing and teaching, or complicate it?
Dickinson keeps the Sabbath at home and Paine’s mind is his church. What do readings 32 to 34 say a person loses who takes the spirit and leaves the form?

Acton, Madison and Montesquieu assume that those who hold authority will be tempted to misuse it. Which safeguards do the readings rely on (see 38, 43 to 45, 56 and 57), and are they of the same kind?
“We have this treasure in earthen vessels.” How should a member respond when the instruments are imperfect, according to readings 46 to 48, and what keeps that patience from becoming complacency?
The guide ends by offering the Bahá’í experience “as a model for study”. What would an outside student want to see before taking the model seriously (reading 51)?

outside.why: “Any agency whatever … is capable of misuse.” Lord Acton’s sentence about every office held by men: power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.
Madison drew the constitutional conclusion: if men were angels, no government would be necessary; since they are not, government must be obliged to control itself.
An excellent thing diverted to wrong ends is still excellent. Jesus on the teachers who sit in Moses’ seat: what they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works.
Blake found a chapel built in the Garden of Love, with “Thou shalt not” over the door. For him the misuse is the institution. On what grounds does the reading hold the two apart?
A meeting should be spiritual and “as formless as possible”. Paul’s picture of worship at Corinth: every one hath a psalm, a doctrine, a revelation; let all things be done unto edifying.
The same chapter ends: let all things be done decently and in order. Paul had seen what formlessness did at Corinth. How much form does a meeting need for all to be edified?
“Do not worship the Lantern—worship the light.” Neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem: the true worshippers shall worship in spirit and in truth.
A foundation beside which other causes are toys, because it is “the spirit of the world”. Except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it.
A new assembly, small as yet. Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
Following “the hard and fixed letter” deprives the law of its spirit. The letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.
Forms and practices “are but garments”. The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath.
Religion is not “confined in an edifice”. Paul at Athens: God dwelleth not in temples made with hands.

Emily Dickinson keeps the Sabbath staying at home, with a bobolink for a chorister. If religion is an attitude reflected through life, why is she not simply right, and the rest of this guide unnecessary?
What the Book does not state is open. Paul on such matters: let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
Convey the message, and do not multiply committees. Matthew Arnold called faith in machinery the besetting danger of his countrymen: machinery valued as if it were an end in itself.

What made the apostles succeed: organizing, or prayer and teaching? Acts shows them choosing: seven are appointed to the daily tables so that the twelve may give themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word. They did organize, in order not to be organizers.
A spiritual gathering has no connection with material matters. Make not my Father’s house an house of merchandise.
Houses of Justice “must attain to the potency to be such”. First the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear.
Some play the dervish in streets and markets. Paul to idlers in an expectant church: if any would not work, neither should he eat; with quietness let them work.
No paid ministers, no clergy, no popes. Be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master; and all ye are brethren.
When two men prophesy in the camp without leave, Moses refuses to stop them: would God that all the Lord’s people were prophets.
Milton on a hireling clergy: the hungry sheep look up, and are not fed.
When money is argued over, people “loose their spiritual fragrance”. The love of money is the root of all evil.
No centralization in the future, but a federation of free peoples. Kant argued the same for perpetual peace: a federation of states, since a universal monarchy would be a soulless despotism.
Efficiency must be accompanied by love and devotion: to separate them “is to deaden the body of the Cause”. As the body without the spirit is dead.
Believers must understand the administration. Jethro to Moses: provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth.
The Faith “cannot be confined to a mere system of organization”. Ezekiel’s bones come together, sinew and flesh, but there is no breath in them until the prophet calls the wind.
A perfect order cut off from the channels of the Spirit would avail nothing. Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
Watch “lest undue concern for the minute details” eclipse the purpose. Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: but one thing is needful.
The tool must not supersede the Faith. Ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law.

Administration exists to strengthen the teaching work, “never … an end in itself”. A candlestick exists for the candle; yet men do not light a candle and leave it without one. What does a lamp need a stand for?
Administration is to help a new mode of community life to emerge. Luke’s sketch of the first community: steadfast in fellowship, in breaking of bread and in prayers.
What exists now is “only the first shaping”. When I was a child, I spake as a child.
Young communities, eager to administer, forget love. And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.

The administrative order is said to derive from the Founder’s own Will and not to be a later imposition. The Church has claimed the same from one sentence about a rock and keys. What makes such a claim testable?
Unlike earlier dispensations, laws and institutions were laid down in writing. Moses wrote the law in a book and had it placed beside the ark as a witness.
A world-wide and complex cause needs coordination. Jethro, watching Moses judge alone from morning to evening: thou wilt surely wear away; this thing is too heavy for thee.

“Many say do not bind the spirit with institutions.” Rousseau: man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains. He, too, went on to design institutions. Is the choice ever between binding and not binding?
Develop the institutions, do not abolish them. New wine must be put into new bottles, and both are preserved.
To accept the Cause is to accept it entire. James on the law: whosoever shall keep the whole, and yet offend in one point, is guilty of all.
Paine: “My own mind is my own church.” The reading denies that one may take the teachings and leave the order. What would Paine have to be shown?
The purpose was not only principles but an order. Daniel’s vision: the God of heaven shall set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed.
Every adherent submits to the considered judgment of Assemblies. Obey them that have the rule over you: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account.

Mill: over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign. The Assemblies’ authority concerns the common affairs of a community one joins freely. Where does Mill’s line fall within that?
The institutions guard continuity and integrity. Jude asks believers to contend for the faith once delivered.
An immutable Word and an elastic administration. Burke: a state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.
Those called to direct the affairs of the Cause are to serve and consult, not dictate. Whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister.
Assemblies should inspire confidence, and believers give it. Confucius ranked the confidence of the people above food and arms: without it a state cannot stand.
Power is unlocked “at the level of individual initiative”. The master gives to every man according to his several ability, and expects each to trade with what he has.

And it “surges at the level of collective volition”. Tocqueville saw Americans of all ages and conditions constantly forming associations, and thought the art of associating the mother of all progress.
Earlier ages wanted “every question answered”. The secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us.
Do not overload believers with rules. The council of Jerusalem: to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things.
They bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders.
Be fearful of too many rules; the Cause is not so fragile. Stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
“The system is perfect, but … the instruments are imperfect.” We have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.
The Assemblies are “patterns for the future”, however inadequate now. Hebrews speaks of a tabernacle made as the example and shadow of heavenly things.
Public attention makes it imperative for institutions to improve. The early Church’s list for an overseer begins: blameless, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour.
Numbers do not measure progress. Gideon is told that the people with him are too many, lest Israel vaunt themselves.
The public must see “a true pattern, in action”. Tertullian reports what pagans said of the Christians: see how they love one another.
The machinery serves expansion and internal consolidation. The whole body fitly joined together, every part working, maketh increase unto the edifying of itself in love.

Authority is concentrated in the National Assembly and power in the local ones. Montesquieu: when the legislative and executive powers are united in the same body, there can be no liberty. What in the readings stands where his separation of powers stands?
A balance between centralization and decentralization. Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
“It is not fair that a kingdom rules by means of a single point.” Samuel warns Israel what a king will take: sons, daughters, fields, a tenth of everything.
Mill: a State which dwarfs its men, in order that they may be more docile instruments in its hands, will find that with small men no great thing can really be accomplished.
The order does not suppress diversity of origin, language and habit. Kallen’s figure for such a commonwealth is an orchestra, each people an instrument with its own timbre.
The Lesser Peace will come by decision of governments. Tennyson’s vision of 1842: the war-drum throbs no longer, in the Parliament of man, the Federation of the world.
No lesser machinery can bring enduring peace. Isaiah’s nations beat their swords into plowshares when the law goes forth and He judges among them.
The Bahá’í experience is offered “as a model for study”. UNESCO’s constitution begins from the same modesty about treaties: it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed.
